original_question: Call a body V in R^3 an optical fiber if it is bounded by two plane figures F1 and F2 together with a smooth tube Σ, and every light ray entering V through one end and reflecting perfectly on the interior walls exits through the other end with probability 1, while every light ray starting inside V exits through one of the ends with probability 1. Must every such optical fiber admit a slicing into plane figures that meet the walls at right angles?
target_in_paper: Section 17, "Optical fibers": the main open problem asking whether every optical fiber can be sliced into plane figures that meet the walls at right angles.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's actual question. It has the correct ambient space R^3, the correct geometric setup of a bounded body with two planar ends and a smooth tube, the correct billiard-style perfect-reflection hypothesis, the additional almost-sure escape condition for rays starting inside, and the correct target question about slicing into plane figures meeting the walls at right angles.
missing_details: The paper asks this specifically as the concrete reformulation of whether there are any optical-fiber constructions other than the standard one obtained by transporting a fixed plane figure along a smooth curve using a parallel normal frame.
To be fully paper-faithful, the question should retain the paper's term "optical fiber" exactly for bodies satisfying both almost-sure transport and almost-sure eventual escape conditions.
The intended slicing is not just one planar cut, but a slicing of the whole body into plane figures meeting the wall orthogonally.

The paper leaves "with probability 1" informal; it does not specify a formal probability space or invariant measure on initial rays, so a stand-alone rewrite should not pretend that extra formalism is supplied in the paper.
The follow-up question about noncongruent ends is separate in the paper and should not replace the main slicing question, though it explains the motivation.
refined_question: Let V be a bounded body in R^3 whose boundary consists of two plane figures F1 and F2 (the ends) and a smooth surface Sigma (the tube). Assume that V is an optical fiber in the sense of Section 17: a light ray entering V through one end and reflecting perfectly from the interior wall exits through the other end with probability 1, and any light ray starting in the interior of V exits through one of the two ends with probability 1. Must every such optical fiber admit a slicing into plane figures that meet the walls at right angles?
justification: The draft is already essentially the paper's main Section 17 problem. I only tightened it by aligning it with the paper's exact setup and by keeping the slicing question as the primary target. In Section 17, Petrunin first defines an optical fiber, then recalls the standard parallel-normal-frame construction, and then asks the slicing question as the official formulation of whether there are any genuinely different constructions. I did not replace the target by the nearby question about noncongruent ends, because the paper presents that only as a separate "In particular" follow-up.
